item.title: [UX Collective 🇧🇷 (artigos)] Onboarding de um programa de divulgadores pela visão de UX
item.description:
Bastidores de um projeto de UX Writing em que a maior parte das pessoas desistia antes de abrir a própria loja.

Uma coisa quem trabalha com produto sabe: ninguém desiste de um cadastro porque tem preguiça.

Eu vi isso de perto num projeto que fiz e que tenho carinho até hoje. Trabalhei no redesenho do onboarding de um programa de divulgadores de um grande e-commerce brasileiro. É um programa em que pessoas físicas abrem uma loja online gratuita, divulgam produtos nas redes sociais e ganham comissão pelas vendas. A empresa cuida de pagamento, entrega e pós-venda e a pessoa é basicamente uma divulgadora/afiliada.

Parece simples, né? Abre a loja, compartilha o link, vende.

Só que os números contavam outra história: a maior parte de quem chegava na página de cadastro não chegava ao fim dele.

Neste texto, conto como a gente investigou esse funil, o que descobrimos e por que boa parte da solução estava nas palavras.

Por questões de confidencialidade, troquei nomes, números e detalhes internos.

­

O que é um onboarding?

Onboarding é o caminho que leva alguém de “quero experimentar” até “consegui usar”.

No nosso caso, era o trecho entre a pessoa clicar em Criar minha loja e ver a própria loja no ar, pronta para vender.

No glossário que construímos para o time, a definição dizia que:

O onboarding precisa guiar a pessoa, detalhando e coletando as informações necessárias para que ela siga sem interferências.

Onboarding é a primeira conversa que um produto tem com alguém.

­

O diagnóstico mostrou um funil que vazava em vários pontos

A primeira coisa que fizemos foi parar de achar e começar a olhar. Mapeamos o fluxo inteiro, separando as portas de entrada, porque a pessoa não chega ao cadastro sempre do mesmo jeito:

  • Tráfego orgânico: a pessoa deveria cair na landing page do programa, mas às vezes caía na página raiz ou até numa página antiga, de quando o programa tinha outro nome.
  • Anúncio pago em rede social: aqui a pessoa pulava a landing page inteira. Ela chegava ao cadastro só com o que tinha lido no criativo do anúncio, sem contexto.
  • Quem já era cliente do e-commerce: se o CPF já tinha login na loja, a pessoa podia usar o mesmo usuário e senha e pular etapas. Ótimo na teoria, mas extremamente confuso na prática (já já explico).

Olhando o fluxo com calma, apareceram padrões que valiam para todas as entradas:

  1. A indicação de etapas não funcionava. A pessoa não sabia em que ponto do cadastro estava nem quanto faltava.
  2. Uma das etapas quase não era usada. Era um passo de montar a vitrine da loja, que pouca gente completava.
  3. O vídeo explicativo ficava fora do fluxo. E muita gente precisava assistir mais de uma vez para conseguir terminar o cadastro.
  4. O primeiro acesso à loja não orientava nada. A pessoa terminava o cadastro e caía numa tela sem um próximo passo claro.

Na landing page, o mapa de calor mostrou duas coisas curiosas:

  1. A área mais quente era uma calculadora de comissões. PLIM! As pessoas queriam muito entender quanto poderiam ganhar, mas não havia nenhum botão de criar loja perto dela. O desejo estava ali, e a porta, longe.
  2. A outra área quente era o botão Entrar, sinal de que a página também funcionava como ponto de login para quem já era divulgador.

O que usuários falaram e nós escutamos

Dois relatos mudaram a forma como enxerguei o projeto.

O primeiro foi de alguém que viu uma mensagem dizendo que já tinha uma conta cadastrada. A pessoa achou que era uma conta do programa de divulgadores, quando, na verdade, o sistema estava falando da conta dela como cliente do e-commerce.

Mesma palavra, dois significados.
Resultado: confusão e abandono.

O segundo foi sobre o nome da loja. O texto dizia algo sobre a possibilidade de troca, mas a pessoa não conseguia entender se podia trocar uma vez, se só podia trocar no primeiro dia ou se não podia trocar nunca.

Quando a regra não fica clara, a pessoa trava, porque ninguém quer escolher um nome “pra sempre” sem ter certeza.

Repara que nenhum dos dois problemas era de tecnologia, eram problemas de linguagem.

­

Antes e depois: o texto como ponte

Agora, a parte que mais gosto de mostrar!

Com a chegada de um login unificado, uma única conta para acessar o e-commerce e o painel do divulgador, precisávamos avisar milhares de pessoas que o jeito de entrar tinha mudado. Para preservar a confidencialidade, chamo aqui de “ID da Loja”.

O que mudou, na prática:

  • Saiu a comparação que confundia. Chamar o ID de “uma senha única” misturava dois conceitos. Um ID não é uma senha, é uma chave de acesso. A metáfora errada cria a dúvida que era necessário evitar.
  • Saiu o “é obrigatório… tudo bem?”. A frase transferia para a pessoa a responsabilidade de garantir que as contas batessem. Na nova versão, o próprio sistema já traz o usuário preenchido. A regra virou ajuda.
  • A ação virou passo a passo com duas etapas, uma ação por linha. A pessoa sabe onde está e quanto falta .
  • O texto ficou mais curto sem perder calor. Falamos do benefício de ter um acesso mais rápido e seguro.

O mesmo cuidado entrou em telas menores. A recuperação de senha, que antes abria com “Esqueceu a senha?”, ganhou um tom mais neutro e direto: “Para acessar, informe o e-mail cadastrado.”

Pode parecer detalhe, mas perguntar “esqueceu?” logo de cara aponta o dedo para a pessoa e falar da ação aponta o caminho.

­

O glossário: a decisão invisível que sustenta todas as outras

Lembra do relato da pessoa que confundiu “conta de cliente” com “conta de divulgador”? Ele nasceu de um problema maior: cada time chamava as coisas de um jeito. Seller, divulgador, parceiro, loja, lojinha, vitrine, painel… Tudo isso circulava nas telas, nos e-mails e nas mensagens de suporte, sem padrão.

Por isso, um dos entregáveis do projeto foi um glossário do programa, uma lista viva com os termos que usamos, o que eles significam e como falar sobre eles com quem divulga. Algumas decisões que saíram dali:

  • “Divulgador” passou a ser o nome oficial de quem tem uma loja no programa, em vez de termos genéricos.
  • “Loja do divulgador” ficou definida como o espaço onde a pessoa vende, busca ofertas, monta vitrines e divulga.
  • “Lojinha” foi vetada. O diminutivo soa pejorativo. A loja de alguém que está construindo uma renda extra é uma loja… e merece ser chamada assim.

­

Se você vai redesenhar um onboarding amanhã, comece por aqui

Um passo a passo para aplicar já, no seu produto:

  1. Mapeie todas as portas de entrada. Quem vem de anúncio sabe menos do que quem leu a landing page. O texto precisa compensar essa diferença.
  2. Junte dados e relatos. O funil mostra onde a pessoa desiste; o relato mostra o porquê. Um sem o outro conta meia história.
  3. Caçe palavras com duplo sentido. “Conta”, “cadastro”, “acesso”: se a mesma palavra nomeia duas coisas, uma delas precisa de outro nome.
  4. Transforme regras em instruções. Em vez de “é obrigatório que…”, diga o que fazer ou faça o sistema resolver por ela.
  5. Mostre o caminho. Etapas numeradas, uma ação por vez, e um aviso claro de quanto falta.
  6. Crie (ou atualize) um glossário. A consistência da linguagem é o que impede o próximo relato confuso.
  7. Assista às pessoas usando. Uma gravação de alguém tentando cadastrar vale mais que dez reuniões de alinhamento.

E por aí, como trabalham em casos de Onboarding?

item.title: [UX Collective] UI edge cases: A reference guide
item.description:
A practical reference guide for catching UI edge cases before they ship — organized by category, with how to test, how to detect them in the wild, and how to design a fix. With examples.

Introduction

One day my colleague and I were at a workshop in a client’s office about agentic workflows in UI Design and Development when suddenly the client asked us a very good question.

“If we, designers and developers, are left to check the AI’s code for all the small but important edge cases it might miss — why don’t we give a document or a list of UI edge cases to the AI to begin with?”

Indeed a very good question, so my colleague and I tasked ourselves with finding a document like this so we could send it to our client.

But we couldn’t find anything that was generic enough to fit every client and specific enough to include all the little cases we saw everyday. Between us we have more than 15 years of UI Design and Development background.

We did find a few documents that had some of the information we needed as well as some that were industry-specific like documents for the Military, Governments, Medical or Telecom.

In the end I was tasked with writing a comprehensive document and sending it to the client for approval and it did end up giving the agentic workflow better results in terms of code generation.

So in the name of sharing, I give here the full document paraphrased in human language with some of the more technical code left out to keep it as generic and readable as possible.

1. Content-Driven

Empty states

This can happen when there’s no data to show yet, zero search results, empty inbox, empty list — screen looks broken or unfinished with no explanation.

To test, load the page with a brand-new account or a filtered view that returns nothing, or manually clear a list’s data source.

The solution is to design and implement a dedicated empty state — icon / illustration, one-line explanation, a clear next action (e.g., “No projects yet — Create one”).

Text length extremes

Long names or titles that break the layout (overflow, wrapping into other elements), very short or single-character values might look off-balance.

We can use pseudo-localization or seed test data with a deliberately long string (e.g., “Supercalifragilisticexpialidocious International Holdings LLC”) and a 1 or 2 character string in every text field, like “I” or “OK”.

We can solve this by defining truncation rules per component (single-line ellipsis vs. multi-line clamp vs. wrap) and set max-widths.

Long unbroken strings

URLs, emails, or IDs don’t wrap, causing horizontal overflow or breaking the container. A user might paste a long URL or a 40+ character token into any field that renders user content.

We should decide whether to truncate mid-string (common for hashes / emails) with an ellipsis in the middle, or just allow wrapping.

Pluralization and zero counts

Wordings like “1 items” or “0 item” can read as broken or unpolished. Some languages have more plural forms than English (Russian, Arabic).

Force counts of 0, 1, 2, and a large number through any relevant component, test with a locale that has more complex plural rules if you plan to localize.

To solve this we need to explicitly copy-write the 0, 1, and many states rather than assuming one template covers all of them. On the development side, we can use an i18n library with proper pluralization.

Localization / i18n

Translated text can run up to 40% longer (German, Finnish) or even run shorter, breaking fixed-width buttons and labels. RTL languages (Arabic, Hebrew) often need mirrored layouts while dates, numbers and currency formats vary.

We can pseudo-localize the UI (wrap strings with padding characters) to simulate expansion using a toggle with dir=”rtl” and browse the whole flow, try switching OS and browser locale when possible.

Design components with flexible widths, not fixed pixel widths for text containers, RTL “mirrored” variants for directional icons (arrows, chevrons and more) and “mirrored” interactions if relevant.
On the development side use logical CSS properties (margin-inline-start instead of margin-left) so RTL can be flipped automatically.

Missing media

Broken image links, users with no avatar, videos that failed to load — leaves a broken-image icon or an unintended blank space.

You can point an <img> src at a 404 URL (an address you know that doesn’t exist) to test this. Also test a user record with a null avatar field, a throttled network to successfully fail media loads.

Design a fallback state — initials-based avatar when image fails to load, or a generic placeholder image, a poster frame for a failed video.

2. State-Driven

Loading states

A blank screen or jarring pop-in while data loads — unclear if the app is frozen or if loading takes too long.

We can throttle network to “Slow 3G” in devtools and artificially delay API responses in a staging environment.

Design skeleton screens that match final content’s shape (not just generic spinners) for anything that takes >300ms and define a timeout state (“This is taking longer than usual”).

Error states

Network failures, validation errors, or partial failures (some data loaded, some didn’t) show up as a blank screen, console-only error, or generic “Something went wrong.”

Kill the network mid-request, mock a 500 / 403 / timeout response, simulate a request where only some of several parallel calls fail.

We should design distinct states per error type (network vs. permission vs. validation) with actionable recovery (a retry button, send bug report etc).

Interim / optimistic states

The gap between user action and server confirmation is either invisible (user might be unsure if it worked) or the UI update is later reverted, thus confusing the user.

We can add artificial latency and watch what the UI displays between click and response, we can force the server call to fail after an optimistic update to see the rollback behavior. Review any “like / save / delete” style interaction.

Define a clear pending visual, such as: subtle dimming, spinner on a specific element (not the whole page) and a clear rollback / error treatment if it fails / succeeds.

Permission / auth states

Logged-out views, session expiring mid-action, or insufficient permissions leads to silent failures or confusing redirects.

We can expire a session token manually and attempt an action, log in as a lower-permission role and attempt a restricted action, test deep-linking to a protected page while logged out.

Design a “session expired” interstitial that preserves the user’s in-progress work where possible, also design disabled / hidden variants for restricted actions with an explanation on hover or on tap.

Stale data

User might leave a tab open for hours, underlying data changes (deleted by someone else or otherwise updated elsewhere) and the UI still reflects the older state, leading to conflicting edits.

To test this — try to open the same record in two sessions, edit in one, then act on the other without refreshing.

We should design a “this has changed” banner with a refresh or merge actions rather than silently overwriting the tab, which can be jarring.

3. Input-Driven

Focus states

Keyboard-only users can’t tell what’s in focus. Focus can get trapped or lost when opening / closing modals or menus.

Try unplugging the mouse and navigate the entire flow with Tab / Shift+Tab / Enter / Space / Escape only.

Design a visible, high-contrast focus ring as a first-class state for every interactive element (don’t rely on browser defaults, but don’t remove it completely either).

Disabled / readonly variations

Disabled and readonly states might look identical, or aren’t visually distinguishable enough from enabled states, this can confuse users about why they can’t interact with some elements.

Try Placing a disabled, readonly, and enabled version of the same component side by side, or next to a simliar looking component, and see if a new user can tell them apart without any documentation (for example a primary disabled button next to an enabled secondary button).

Give the disabled and readonly states a distinct, documented visual treatment (for example: disabled = grayed + no cursor change. Readonly = normal color + lock icon).

Rapid / repeated input

Users might double-click a submit button and it shouldn’t fire duplicate requests (double charge, duplicate record, etc.), spamming a button or rapid resize / scroll causes jank or race conditions.

Try rapidly double-click and triple-click every button, hold down a resize handle and drag erratically, scroll-flick a long list repeatedly.

Show an immediate disabled / loading / read-only state on the button or input field the instant it was clicked.

Copy-paste

A pasted text can carry unexpected formatting, emojis, or control characters that break layout, validation, or storage.

Try to copy rich text from a Word doc or a webpage and paste it into every text input or text area. Paste emoji-heavy text and right-to-left text. Paste a string with null bytes or control characters.

Decide whether inputs even should accept formatting (a rich text field) or strip it (a plain text field) and be consistent per field type or style.

4. Layout / Responsive

Extreme viewport sizes

Very narrow screens (folded phones, for example) or very wide monitors (ultrawide, 3440px+) can break layouts designed for a “typical” resolution range.

Resize the browser window to its minimum and to full ultrawide width, you can use devtools device emulation for specific devices or screen sizes.

Design with min-width / max-width content in mind, don’t let a single-column layout stretch to a full-width column on an ultrawide display. Don’t let content collapse below a usable minimum either.

Zoom levels

Try zoom the browser to 200% or use OS text-scaling to break the layout, this can create overlapping texts and cut-off buttons.

Zoom browser to 200% (a WCAG requirement) and navigate the full flow. Increase or decrease OS-level text size setting.

Design with relative units in mind so text scaling doesn’t require pixel-perfect fixed layouts, otherwise near-sighted users may be unable to use your website.

Dynamic content changing dimensions

A component resizing based on content (for example: an accordion, a comment with a long reply) can push neighboring elements around unexpectedly, causing a layout shift.

Try to trigger the resize (expand accordion, load async content, change dynamic content) and watch for neighboring elements jumping, you can also check Lighthouse’s Cumulative Layout Shift score.

To accomodate this, please reserve space or use smooth height transitions rather than instant jumps. Consider whether the expanding element should overlay instead of pushing the content.

Nested scroll containers

Scroll-within-scroll creates ambiguous scroll targeting (users might scroll the page when they meant scrolling the inner panel, or vice versa).

Sticky elements can overlap or conflict, horizontally-scrollable components (carousels, tables) nested in a vertically-scrolling page can hijack diagonal trackpad / touch gestures, or unintentionally introduce page-level horizontal scrolling if content overflows without being contained.

We can scroll with our cursor at the boundary between inner and outer scrolling areas. We can test using a trackpad, a mouse wheel, and touch input separately (they can behave differently).

Also check for an unexpected horizontal scrollbar on the page itself by resizing the viewport narrower than the widest nested element.

Minimize nested scroll where possible. If necessary, give the inner scroll area a clear visual boundary so users can know which scroll will be captured. Avoid mixing scroll axes in adjacent / nested regions where possible.

Safe areas

Take into consideration notches, browser chrome, and virtual keyboards covering content or inputs, especially on mobile.

Test on an actual notched device (or simulator) in both orientations, also focus a text input near the bottom of the screen and check if the keyboard covers it or shifting the view to reveal it.

Try to keep critical content and actions out of the extreme edges. Design for a keyboard-visible state on forms when possible.

5. System / Environment

Dark mode / forced-colors / high contrast

Custom-styled components (checkboxes, radio buttons, focus rings) lose their custom styling or become invisible in forced-colors / high-contrast modes. Dark mode might reveal hardcoded colors that don’t adapt.

Toggle OS-level dark mode and Windows High Contrast Mode. Test with devtools prefers-color-scheme: dark / light.

Define a full dark-mode palette (not just an inverted light mode) and verify contrast ratios in both modes.

Reduced motion preference

Some users have stated preference for reduced motion and they still get full animations, which can cause discomfort or eye strain.

Try to enable “Reduce Motion” in OS accessibility settings and revisit all animated interactions in your site, does it still animate or do you see a fallback instead?

We should design a reduced-motion variant for key animations like cross-fading instead of slides and zooms, or instant state changes instead of complex movement.

Font-loading flash (FOUT / FOIT)

FOUT is the Flash of unstyled text and FOIT is the Flash of invisible text, both can happen while custom web fonts load, often times with a layout shift when the font swaps.

Throttle your network in devtools and reload the page. Compare fallback font metrics to the final font. Lighthouse flags font-display issues and layout shift from font swap.

We can try and choose a fallback font with similar x-height / width to the custom font to minimize the layout shift, or we can choose to hide the text itself until the font loads.

Offline / flaky connectivity

When a user is on a flaky network, the app might appear frozen or throws unhandled errors when the network drops or is intermittent.

Please use the devtools to simulate “Offline” mid-session. Use a network-throttling proxy to simulate packet loss or a flaky connection.

Design an offline banner / indicator and, if feasible, an offline-capable mode (view cached data, queue actions, local host etc).

Closing thoughts

I hope this list can be the bare-minimum standard of UI edge cases that are checked and taken care of, from localization to error states to offline mode, there’s no reason to leave them out anymore.

Next year I’m sure we’ll have more edge cases that will pop up once those are already fixed, I have high hopes for this industry that with the emergence of AI the standard for good software will only get higher.

If this list made you, or your AI, spit out more usable code or a better thought out product overall, please share this article online.

Thanks for reading, and I’d love to hear your experience in the comments, also if I missed any edge cases — please tell me and I’ll roll it into the next version of this article.

item.title: [UX Planet] Information Visualization: 6 Essential Rules Every Designer Should Know
item.description:
How to turn complex data into clear, meaningful, and actionable visualizations

We live in a world where organizations collect enormous amounts of data. But collecting data and understanding it are two very different things. And this problem becomes even more noticable in the context of dashboards that org create: a dashboard might contain dozens of charts and hundreds of data points, yet still fail to answer the fundamental question:

What should I do with this information?

And, unfortunately, with the rise of AI tools this problem becomes more and more important because data visualization design now is easier than ever, but not many people who create dashboards understand the principles behind good visualization.

Information visualization is a discipline that aims to answer this question. In this article, I’ll explain what information visualization is and share 6 practical rules for creating effective information visualizations.

What is information visualization?

Information visualization is transforming complex data into visual representations that help people understand patterns, identify problems, and make better decisions.

1. Start with the question, not the chart

One of the most common mistakes designers make is focusing too much on visual appearance of data vis and forgetting functional purpose that it serves. As a result, they focus too much on selecting a chart type before understanding what users actually need to know.

For example, imagine you’re designing a sales dashboard. You have revenue data for the last 12 months. You could show it as a bar chart, a line chart, or a table. But the right choice depends on the question:

  • How much revenue did we generate? Show a prominent number.
  • How has revenue changed over time? Use a line chart.
  • Which product generates the most revenue? Use a ranked bar chart.
  • Why is revenue declining? Show contributing factors such as cancellations, returns, or lower conversion rates.

Thats why the first rule is so simple:

Define the decision your visualization should support before choosing how to represent the data.

2. Design for human perception

Good information visualization is based on how the human brain processes visual information. Our brain can quickly recognize differences in position, length, size, and color. Designers can use these properties to help people identify important information without consciously examining every data point.

For example, imagine a dashboard with 20 indicators. If every indicator has the same visual weight, users need to examine each one to find what’s important. But if the two most critical metrics are larger and visually prominent, users can immediately focus on them.

You can also apply Gestalt principles, such as proximity and similarity, to group related information.

Use visual hierarchy, grouping, and contrast to direct attention toward information that matters.

3. Choose the right visual representation

Not all charts are equally effective at communicating a particular type of information:

  • A pie chart can communicate simple proportions, but it becomes difficult to interpret when it contains too many segments.
  • A bar chart is usually more effective when users need to compare values across categories.
  • A line chart works well for showing changes over time.
  • And a network diagram helps visualize relationships between connected entities.

You need to match the visualization to the structure of the data and the task users need to perform.

Choose charts based on what insights users need to extract from data, not on which visualization looks most impressive.

4. Reduce information overload

One of the biggest problems with modern systems (including dashboards) is that designers try to display everything at once. But more data doesn’t necessarily produce better insights.

The signals often result in complete for human attention.

A better approach is to information priorization and, if you need to provide more information, use progressive disclosure (aka offer additional details on demand).

The approach I follow is simple:

  1. Start by presenting the most important information up front.
  2. Then allow users to explore additional details when necessary.

For example, a revenue dashboard might initially display three key metrics: Total revenue, Net profit and Revenue growth. Give users an option to drill down into specific regions, products, or time periods.

Another important consideration is removing chartjunk (decorative visual elements that don’t improve understanding).

Unnecessary 3D effects, heavy gradients, excessive gridlines, and decorative illustrations can make visualizations harder to read.

Every visual element should contribute to understanding the data. If it doesn’t, consider removing it.

5. Make visualizations interactive when necessary

Static charts are useful when everyone needs to see the same information. But when users have different questions or need to investigate complex data, interaction becomes valuable.

For example, an interactive sales dashboard might allow users to:

  • Filter revenue by product category.
  • Compare performance across different periods.
  • Drill down into individual transactions.
  • Explore relationships between multiple metrics.

But similar to any design decision, interaction should always serve a clear purpose. If you add dozens of filters and controls assuming users will need, can easily create more complexity than value.

Introduce interaction when it helps users answer questions that a static visualization cannot.

6. Evaluate whether your visualization actually works

You are not your user ©

A visualization that looks perfectly clear to you (its creator) can be confusing to everyone else. That’s why evaluation is an essential part of the design process.

You don’t necessarily need a large usability study to identify problems.

Start by showing your visualization to a few people (2–3 people who represent your target audience)

Ask them questions such as:

  • What is the most important information on this screen?
  • What conclusions can you draw from this chart?
  • Can you identify any unusual trends?
  • What action would you take based on this information?

Pay attention to whether users interpret the visualization correctly, how quickly they find answers, and where they struggle.

Don’t evaluate visualizations solely; evaluate how effectively it works for your target audience

Want to master information visualization?

If you want to go beyond the basics, I recommend exploring the Information Visualization course by the Interaction Design Foundation (IxDF). The course covers human visual perception and memory, Gestalt principles, visual mapping, advanced techniques for representing complex data, and methods for evaluating visualizations.

item.title: [UX Stack Exchange] How do I keep research quality high when designers and PMs run usability and concept tests themselves?
item.description:
I work at an early-stage startup, and I’m the only person with a research background. The company can’t afford a researcher for every team, so designers and product managers do a lot of their own research, and I’m often asked to “get research done” through them.

In practice, that mostly means two things. Designers run usability tests on prototypes before handing them to engineering, usually five or six sessions over a couple of days. And PMs run concept tests, where they show an early idea or mockup to a handful of customers and ask whether they’d use it.

I’m glad they’re doing it, but I keep noticing the same problems. In a recent usability test, the designer helped participants when they got stuck (“oh, you can click here”) and then counted the task as a success. In a concept test, the PM asked “would you use something like this?”, got a few polite yeses, and took that as validation. Sample sizes are small, notes are inconsistent, and the findings tend to confirm what the team already wanted to build.

I don’t want to be the person who slows everyone down or tells them their research doesn’t count. But I also don’t want product decisions made on weak evidence.

So my questions are:

  • Is there an established framework or guide for keeping quality up when non-researchers run studies like these?
  • What should stay with a researcher, and what is safe to hand off?
  • What support (templates, review, training) makes the biggest difference in practice, especially for a one-person research function?

item.title: [UX Collective] Decision theatre or decision design?
item.description:
AI has made information easy, but it has not made decisions simple. As machines produce more than we can read, our job is shifting from building knowledge to owning decisions. Are we ready?

In a 2025 survey by BetterUp Labs and the Stanford Social Media Lab, 40% of US desk workers said they had received workslop in the previous month: AI-generated work that looks polished but does not move the task forward. Respondents reported spending nearly two hours, on average, dealing with each incident.

Imagine a team of ten, each receiving one piece of workslop a month. That is roughly 20 hours, more than two working days, spent cleaning up someone else’s shortcut.

We have never produced so much data, so many documents, decks and summaries. And we have never produced so much digital waste.

This is a productivity problem, but it is also a symptom.

The question is not how much faster we can produce something. It is how much extra work that production creates for everyone else, and who is left to decide what any of it means.

How did we get here?

For most of human history, change moved slowly. Roughly ten thousand years separated the birth of farming from industrialisation. Evolution had time to move from one stage to the next, across centuries and generations.

Then the interval shrank. Only about two centuries separated the first factories from the rise of service and knowledge economies.

And then it shrank again. In 1969, ARPANET connected its first computers: the beginning of the information society. Less than sixty years later, AI agents use the knowledge we put online to make recommendations and, more and more… decisions.

Think about what we did in those sixty years. We created the bits. We built digital worlds and a digital culture. We ran digitalisation programmes. We put books online with Project Gutenberg, information online with Wikipedia. We worked hard to make information accessible and ubiquitous, on every channel, for everyone.

Without knowing it, we were laying the foundation for an artificial form of intelligence to learn from our human-built infrastructure, and to work on top of it.

The information society was basically the training ground for AI. Our knowledge is now the bridge between the old, human-driven world and a new, AI-empowered one.

This compression raises a pressing question.
How quickly can people, organisations and institutions adapt?

Does more information make us wiser?

Not on its own. And we have known that for a long time.

In information management, one of the best-known frameworks is the DIKW pyramid: Data, Information, Knowledge, Wisdom. It is usually credited to Russell Ackoff, who formalised it at the end of the 1980s.

The logic is simple:

  • Data: the raw elements. Facts and signals with no context.
  • Information: data that has been processed and organised.
  • Knowledge: information that has been interpreted and put to use.
  • Wisdom: knowledge that allows judgement.

Each level is built on the one below, but the relationship only works one way. As Steyn puts it, wisdom is always knowledge, but knowledge is not always wisdom. Every level is a subset of the one beneath it.

In 1987, Milan Zeleny proposed the same four levels in a language that organisations understand much better:

  • Know-nothing: data
  • Know-what: information
  • Know-how: knowledge
  • Know-why: wisdom

Read it from the bottom up: each level is built on the one below, but no amount of data adds up to wisdom on its own.

For Zeleny, managing efficiently means knowing how to do things. Managing effectively means knowing what to do. Managing wisely means knowing why. And wisdom goes one step further: it is what lets us compare and judge our know-how and our know-what.

I first wrote about this back in 2013, on LegoViews. Back then, the challenge was getting organisations to make time for that reflection.
Today it is harder. AI hands us endless know-what and know-how in seconds, and reflection, the step that turns them into a shared know-why, is exactly the one we are tempted to skip.

Here is the point that matters most today. Wisdom comes from knowledge, but it is not a sum of knowledge.

Adding knowledge to knowledge does not make wisdom. Processing more information does not make us wiser.

What does AI know, and what doesn’t it?

AI is extraordinary at the bottom of the pyramid. It processes data at a scale no team could match, and it turns that data into know-how: summaries, drafts, analyses, code.

What it cannot settle for us is which problem deserves attention, whose interests should count, and whether we should act on its answer.

These questions depend on context. They put the output into a broader frame: what we are trying to achieve, under which constraints, and why it matters. That frame is where knowledge gets judged.

The worrying part is how many people now trust good-looking information, mistake it for wisdom, and pass it on. Especially in the domains where critical thinking is the whole job.

And even the know-how needs checking. Large language models still add unsupported claims when they summarise a document they were given. On Vectara’s hallucination leaderboard, which tests this, rates in 2026 run from 1.8% to 24.2% of summaries, depending on the model. These are task-specific figures, not universal error rates. But they show how hard it is to rely on AI output that nobody reads closely.

So we have a base of data and good-looking information, produced at a volume that no human can manage.

What are we losing?

For most of my career, the journey from data to judgement had its own pace. And it was work, real work.

We collected an adequate amount of data. We prioritised. We designed studies around sampling and around the constraints we had: time, resources, our ability to analyse, the tools at hand. The constraints forced us to choose, and choosing forced us to think.

Today we are in the middle of a data feast. We access more and more data not because we need it, but because we can.

Slowly, we are creating working conditions in which there is less room to think, prioritise, sequence and distil. Less room for intentionality.

The philosopher John Searle described intentionality as the mind’s capacity to be about something (Intentionality, 1983). In organisations, it takes a more practical shape: the deliberate decision to focus attention and action on a clearly defined purpose. What we are trying to achieve, why it matters, and how our choices serve it.

It is made of a few simple things:

  • Awareness: knowing where we are and what we are looking at.
  • Context: understanding the situation and its variables.
  • Prioritisation: directing attention to what has the most impact.
  • Distillation: separating value from noise.

Without it, we stay in the noise. We consume data because we do not know where we are going, or where we should focus.

All the narratives are about speed. We are omitting the craft.

We stopped trusting the process because we only look at the output. But an output without a process is a simulacrum: something that looks good and has no substance.

What gives value to data and knowledge is not the shape of the output. It is the process that generated it and gave it substance.

Who decides?

AI can do a lot, and it does some things better than we do. But there is one thing it cannot do: be held accountable.

The idea is much older than generative AI. A slide said to come from a 1979 IBM internal training warned that “a computer can never be held accountable”, and concluded that a computer should therefore never make a management decision. The original has never been found in IBM’s archives, but the principle has aged remarkably well (more here).

Nearly fifty years later, regulation gives human oversight a concrete organisational form. Article 26(2) of the EU AI Act asks deployers of high-risk AI systems to assign human oversight to people with the necessary competence, training and authority, and to give them the support they need.

So let’s be clear.

An insurance claim. A loan. A place at a school. Access to benefits.

AI can support every one of these decisions. It can sort the files, flag the risks, summarise the evidence. But these decisions must not become a way for organisations to hide responsibility behind a system.

These decisions affect people’s fundamental rights. Behind each one there must be a human with a name, a role, the responsibility, the authority and the skills to make the decision, stand by it, defend it, and answer for the consequences.

That does not relieve the organisation of responsibility for the system, the workflow or the conditions in which that person is expected to decide.

AI can inform. It cannot own.

This is where the paradox emerges: we have the illusion that we are outsourcing more and more work. In reality, our job is becoming that of the AI supervisor: the person in charge of making AI-enabled decisions.

In one sentence: after we digitalised knowledge and built all the infrastructure, our role is no longer only to build knowledge. It is also to take responsibility for how that knowledge informs decisions.

We are moving from the information society to an age of accountability, where we need to embrace our humanity to make decisions about other humans.

Decision theatre or decision design?

Responsible AI needs humans in the loop. That much is agreed. But a human in the loop is not enough on their own.

Put a disengaged, overloaded or alienated person in front of an AI output and you get decision theatre: the illusion that a decision happened when it did not. Someone clicked “approve”. Nobody decided.

We have a decision-making crisis, and more AI output will deepen it unless something changes. Most organisations lack a decision-making operational layer to support the people who must make the decisions.

A real decision needs three conditions:

  • Skills: the competence and training to read the context, the variables and the pre-digested input, and to tell a valid answer from a well-formatted one.
  • Authority: a name, a role and a position that allow the person to override the AI, and the responsibility to own the result.
  • Process: workflows designed to empower decision makers, with the right information, tools and time, and without drowning them in decision fatigue.

Take one away and the decision collapses into theatre.

Who holds the judgement?

It is tempting to map Zeleny’s forms of knowing onto an organisational chart: leadership decides why, management decides what, operations deliver how. But Zeleny was describing forms of knowing, not ranks of people.

The mistake is to confuse the authority to make a decision with the knowledge needed to make it well. A frontline worker may have no say in strategy, yet can be the first to notice when a process is failing or a case does not fit the rules. Research on digitalised frontline work shows that this tacit knowledge and discretion still matter, even where systems automate parts of the process.

Automate that work without asking what judgement it holds, and the organisation loses more than a task.

Imagine a caseworker reviewing benefit claims flagged by an AI system.

In the theatre version, they get hundreds of cases a day. They see a risk score and two buttons. They have no time to open the file, and overriding the system needs their manager’s sign-off. They approve what the machine suggests. On paper, a human was in the loop.

In the designed version, they get fewer cases, prioritised by uncertainty. They see the sources behind each score and the points where the system is least confident. They can override it, and they record why. Their overrides go back to the team that runs the system, so recurring problems can be investigated and corrected.

Same person. Same AI. A completely different decision.

This is where design enters the scene. Somebody has to design these decision-making workflows: to enable, and indeed empower, humans to decide, and to avoid both decision fatigue and decision theatre.

What skills will the human in the loop need?

If humans are expected to own AI-supported decisions, we need to be clear about what that responsibility requires. We need humans who think as humans, not as machines.

What does that mean?

It means humans who understand the problem, the context and the domain. It means humans who understand the AI output and the process that produced it. It means humans who can separate the validity of the content from the polish of the form.

Three families of skills will matter most.

  • Critical judgement: being sceptical, spotting errors, asking where a claim comes from, and noticing what is missing as well as what is there.
  • Sense-making: taking the knowledge we have built and organising it into structures that increase accuracy, logic, relationships and reliability.
  • Human skills: the so-called soft skills, and the hardest to delegate. Empathy for the person on the other side of the decision. The courage to disagree with the machine. The integrity to sign your name under the result.

None of these is new. What is new is that they are no longer a nice-to-have on top of the “real” work.

They are the work.

How do we teach people to decide?

If these skills are the work, we need to teach them differently. People reviewing AI-supported decisions need practice in judging incomplete evidence, recognising exceptions, understanding the context and rules that apply, and explaining what they decided and why. Without that preparation, we risk creating a new assembly line: people processing recommendations and carrying responsibility for decisions they barely have time to examine.

This means rethinking curricula, in schools, universities and workplaces, around a few plain questions:

  • How do we analyse data to tell the what from the why?
  • How do we read a situation as a system, with its relationships, feedback loops and unintended consequences?
  • How do we decide under uncertainty, and how do we stand by that decision?
  • How do we notice when we are being asked to perform a decision rather than make one?

This is why we need much more teaching in complexity theory and systems thinking. Not as niche electives for a few specialists, but as the foundation for anyone who will sign their name under an AI-enabled decision.

In one word: we need to teach judgement.

What’s next

For years, many of us watched design thinking turn into design doing: more output, faster, with less and less time to think. AI can now do the doing faster than any of us.

This is the crossroads.

One road leads to more of the same. More outputs, more workslop, more decisions that only look like decisions.

The other road brings thinking back to the centre. Framing the problem. Understanding the context. Prioritising. Designing the process that turns AI output into a decision a human can own. This is design thinking applied to the most human act of all: deciding about other humans.

References

  • Ackoff, R. L. (1989). From data to wisdom. Journal of Applied Systems Analysis, 16, 3–9.
  • Searle, J. (1983). Intentionality: An Essay in the Philosophy of Mind. Cambridge University Press.
  • Zeleny, M. (1987). Management support systems: towards integrated knowledge management. Human Systems Management, 7(1), 59–70.

Thank you for reading. I write about design, systems and the human side of AI, and I work with organisations that want to get it right. You’ll find more of my work at PatriziaBertini.com.

item.title: [UX Collective 🇧🇷 (artigos)] Os Backrooms do Design System
item.description:
Os espaços liminares do trabalho de design em ambientes complexos.

Existe uma sensação particularmente desconfortável em estar em um lugar que parece familiar, mas que provoca uma sensação de estranhamento. Igual uma paralisia do sono: tudo parece estar no lugar, mas alguma coisa está errada e você não sabe exatamente o que é…

Depois de assistir ao filme Backrooms: um não lugar, percebi que tem algo parecido no trabalho de design em ambientes complexos.

Quero explorar a realidade de profissionais que atuam nesse espaço: como são as adaptações, os improvisos e as decisões que surgem quando nenhum dos sistemas de design existentes oferecem uma resposta completa? Mais do que apontar inconsistências, a intenção é refletir sobre como lidamos com elas e reconhecer esse trabalho como parte importante do design.

Aqui estou falando de ferramentas que não pertencem inteiramente a um sistema de design ou outro, mas existem com interdependência (como uma plataforma integrada dentro da outra, tendo cada uma origem diferente). E ainda temos uma terceira personagem nessa história: a personalização de sistemas de design preestabelecidos.

Para fazer uma alteração simples existem regras, limitações técnicas, contratos, integrações e decisões tomadas antes mesmo de designers chegarem ali. É nesse espaço entre uma coisa e outra que boa parte do trabalho de design acontece nesses ambientes.

Ao trabalhar integrando ferramentas, plataformas e fornecedores, o desafio não é apenas desenhar uma boa interface. É fazer com que coisas que nasceram separadas consigam parecer parte do mesmo ecossistema.

Assim que saí do cinema, o conceito de não-design system me veio à mente.

Um não-design system é um conjunto de decisões que nasceu de dois DS que precisam caminhar juntos.

Se temos mais de um DS para organizar a experiência, o que acontece quando projetamos em situações nas quais nenhum dos sistemas existentes consegue responder completamente?

Organizei a (não) solução em 3 momentos:

1. Convivência: dois sistemas que ocupam o mesmo espaço

Os sistemas têm suas próprias linguagens, componentes, padrões e comportamentos que precisam funcionar dentro de uma mesma experiência.

O problema é que eles não nasceram necessariamente para conversar entre si.
­

2. Adaptação: quando um sistema precisa falar o idioma do outro

Designers podem adaptar componentes, comportamentos e padrões para criar uma experiência mais coerente.

Mas adaptar nem sempre significa preservar. Para aproximar visualmente dois sistemas é preciso abrir mão de características originais.
­

3. Improvisação: quando nenhum dos sistemas tem a resposta

Não existe componente documentado, padrão estabelecido ou solução pronta. É preciso criar algo que funcione dentro daquele contexto, considerando as limitações existentes.

E assim o nosso não-design system ganha vida. Para quem assistiu ao filme, podemos apelidá-lo de Captain Clark dos design systems.

­

Mas o que isso significa?

Significa que existe uma diferença entre a percepção de designers e a percepção do usuário.

Designers conhecem os sistemas de origem, sabem quais componentes foram adaptados, improvisados, como aconteceu a conversa entre tecnologia e negócio e quais foram os trade-offs.

Designers enxergam as costuras, mas o usuário sente os efeitos pela superfície mesmo sem saber explicar o que está fora do lugar.

Não sabe que dois componentes vieram de desenvolvimentos diferentes, mas percebe quando o mesmo tipo de ação funciona de maneiras diferentes em diferentes pontos da jornada.

Tudo parece meio familiar, mas não exatamente. Quase que um vale da estranheza do meio digital.

Será que o objetivo de designers nesses ambientes deve ser eliminar todas essas inconsistências ou aprender a conviver com elas, escolhendo conscientemente quais concessões são aceitáveis e garantem a melhor experiência dentro do que é possível?

A realidade é que existem muitos designers de produto trabalhando em ambientes complexos com mais zonas cinzentas do que os livros, cursos, influenciadores e cases costumam falar sobre.

Quanto mais complexo o ambiente, designers desenham menos telas e mais acordos entre sistemas e áreas.

O verdadeiro trabalho desse tipo de designer aparece quando não existe uma regra clara e sim quando ele chega para ajudar a resolver um ambiente sem uma resposta pronta.

E você? Já trabalhou em um cenário em que múltiplos design systems precisavam entrar em cena juntos? Como lidou com as adaptações, improvisos e concessões necessárias para fazer tudo funcionar?

item.title: [UX Collective] AI is the new old design material
item.description:
Creative makers and builders have always learned their medium by working with it, from grinding pigments to HTML. Models are the next material, and you need to learn them by building.

The field keeps arguing about whether designers should code, as if that question were new.

It’s not new.

Art and design have always been taught through materials, going back centuries.

In the 1390s, the painter Cennino Cennini wrote a handbook that’s still translated today on grinding pigments, and that history still runs through my own family as builders and creators. My mother, Jean Neeman, ground her own pigments as a conservator for the Los Angeles Museum of Art, the Getty and Hearst Castle, and I watched her repair Chinese statues that were over 600 years old with original materials to restore history.

She lived that craft, as I wrote in Everything I Know About UX I Learned From My Parents. I learned print through paste up, developing film for prints, and running film output.

I understand that knowing the material is a timeless need, and most designers I meet don’t understand it, because their tools hide it. We need to respect it as part of the craft.

The reality is that visual tools like Figma and Sketch are an abstraction, and real craft happens in the final mile, working with the material. Great designers have always used the materials they had, and I’ve always written code as part of the job to understand mine.

On the web, that meant HTML, CSS, Javascript and whatever else that made it work. Artificial intelligence is the new material, teaching the same lesson faster.

The designers doing the strongest work with models run them and read the output. That takes sampling code: a loop asking one question over and over until the model’s habits show.

Study the Bauhaus Workshops

In April 1919, Walter Gropius published the founding manifesto of the Bauhaus, and its demand was direct.

As art historian Magdalena Droste explains in The Bauhaus Manifesto, Gropius told architects, sculptors, and painters to turn to the crafts. The curriculum ended in a list of workshops. Students learned wood, metal, glass, and weaving by cutting, bending, and threading them.

Josef Albers made the point with almost nothing. In his preliminary course, Droste notes, students had to make a flat sheet of paper stand on its own, or bend a straight wire until it held its shape.

A drawing can suggest a chair, but only the wood can tell you where it will split.

That habit produced the school’s best-known work. Marcel Breuer headed the carpentry workshop and bent tubular steel into chairs, and Herbert Bayer went on to run the printing and advertising workshop.

They knew their materials because they had worked them. Every new medium since has sent designers back to a bench of some kind, and the last two benches have been made of code.

Hand-Code 1990s Web Pages

The web forced the same return, and it started with a blank file.

In the mid-1990s, the design tool for the web was a text editor: Notepad on Windows, SimpleText on the Mac. You typed tags, saved the file, and reloaded the browser to see what you’d made. My earliest web credit, the Oliver North home page, came out of that era.

Dedicated tools followed quickly, and each one moved the designer a step further from the markup:

  • BBEdit (1992), a Mac text editor that added HTML tools in 1994.
  • HoTMetaL (1994), an early HTML editor that showed where each tag began and ended.
  • PageMill (1995), Adobe’s visual editor for print designers.
  • FrontPage (1995), a visual editor that Microsoft bought in early 1996.
  • HomeSite (1996), a Windows editor built for people who wanted to write the HTML themselves.
  • Dreamweaver (1997), Macromedia’s visual editor.

The designers who got the most out of the visual editors still opened the code underneath. They trusted the canvas only after checking the page in more than one browser.

A visual editor showed one browser’s best case, and the markup showed the rest.

In 2000, John Allsopp wrote A Dao of Web Design for A List Apart, arguing that the control designers knew in print was a product of the printed page’s limits.

Ten years later, ethan marcotte opened Responsive Web Design with a quote from Allsopp. He built a sample page on a fluid grid with flexible images and media queries, then showed the layout changing shape as the window narrowed.

Responsive design came out of a designer’s style sheet, and no mockup would have found it.

Five years later, Frank Chimero gave the idea a name in The Web’s Grain, writing that “every material has a grain, including the web.” He argued that the field’s best techniques grew out of that grain, and that sites built against it come out fragile and awkward.

Test Model Output Variation

Models break the mockup in a new way. A static screen shows one answer, chosen by the designer and usually the good one. A model returns a different answer each time, and that spread is the thing you’re designing for. Call the chosen answer the one-sample mockup: a screen built around the output the model gives on its best day.

In legal tech, where we designed search and summarization, every summary in a mockup was correct, because a designer wrote it.

  • In 2017, Lars Erik Holmquist argued in Intelligence on Tap: Artificial Intelligence as a New Design Material that designers should treat the technology as a material with its own limits.
  • In UX Design Innovation: Challenges for Working with Machine Learning as a Design Material (2017), Graham Dove and colleagues surveyed UX practitioners. They suggested that machine learning had seen little design innovation, possibly because it was a new and difficult material.
  • Qian Yang’s 2020 dissertation at Carnegie Mellon University, Profiling Artificial Intelligence as a Material for User Experience Design, went further. It traced those difficulties to two roots: uncertainty about what a system can do, and the complexity of what it might output.
A mockup is one sample, and the product is the distribution.

The Doherty Threshold entry on UX Guidelines, my own reference site, puts the point where software starts to feel conversational under 400 milliseconds. A static frame can’t show a four-second wait.

Bret Victor built a whole talk, Inventing on Principle (2012), around the idea that creators need an immediate connection to what they create. You find the spread, the misses, and the delays only by running the model again and again.

Code Prototypes Against Models

Josh Clark tied the two eras together in his 2018 talk The New Design Material, calling machine learning “a design material in the same way that HTML and CSS is.”

In Addressing UX Practitioners’ Challenges in Designing ML Applications (2023), K. J. Kevin Feng and David W. McDonald of the University of Washington ran a study with 27 UX practitioners. Each got a tool to build and test simple models while designing an app.

Hands-on experimentation helped them match model behavior to user goals, invent interface features for correcting the model, and spot ethical risks. One participant explained that without testing, you don’t know “how often or in what ways it’s going to error.”

The authors located the bottleneck in fabrication, the stage where models get made, because designers are usually kept away from it. Their tool needed no code at all.

Today, for language models, a few lines of code are the shortest route to the same hands-on access. Geoffrey Litt saw it coming in Malleable software in the age of LLMs (2023), arguing that language models would let ordinary users build small tools from scratch.

Designers have kept themselves at arm’s length from the material, and that distance is the bottleneck they can no longer ignore.

That distance is closing. Figma’s 2026 AI report found that the share of designers participating in development doubled in a year, from 21% to 41%.

Tools like Claude Code, Cursor, and Figma Make let a designer describe a prototype, wire it to a live model, and watch what breaks in a single sitting.

Not every designer agrees that code belongs in the job. Alan Cooper wrote in Should Designers Code? (2017) that “coding is not a skill necessary to be a top notch interaction designer.”

Karri Saarinen of Linear warned in Design Is More Than Code (2025) that production-first habits can erode the thinking behind a design. Both warnings are about code that ships.

Sampling code gets thrown away the same afternoon, and its only job is to show you the material.

Write AI Evaluation Sets

Sampling code doesn’t need to ship. It works like a test bench, and its most valuable output is a record of every case where the model broke the design. Wood doesn’t change its grain overnight, but a model can change with a single provider update.

Engineers already have a name for this file: an evaluation set. Designers are well placed to write it. They know which failures users notice first, like the answer that runs past the edge of its card or the wrong date stated with total confidence.

A design tuned to last month’s model can fail without a single pixel moving.

Four habits turn the record into working practice:

  • Call the model directly. Ask Claude Code or Cursor for a script that sends real product inputs to the model and prints the answers, and read them before you draw a screen.
  • Run each prompt 50 times. Sort the answers by length, tone, and accuracy, then design for the longest and the most wrong rather than the typical one.
  • Bring the spread to review. Put the two worst of the 50 answers beside the mockup in design review, and decide together which ones the screen must survive.
  • Save failures as test cases. Keep every output that broke a layout or misled a user in a shared file, so engineering reruns it whenever the model or prompt changes.

Run the Model First

Gropius moved students out of drawing rooms because drawings hid what materials would do.

Designers on the early web learned the same thing in a text editor, and Marcotte proved it with a working page. The debate over whether designers should code has always been a debate about the material and how close designers can get to it.

For artificial intelligence products, the material is the model’s behavior across thousands of inputs. You won’t find it in a frame on a canvas. You find it by running the model, reading everything that comes back, and keeping the failures somewhere the team can see them.

These days I describe my job as building, and that’s the reason: I can’t design how a model-backed product works until I’ve watched the model work.

Next time your team reviews an artificial intelligence feature, skip the one-sample mockup. Run the prompt 50 times, bring the worst answer to the review, and design the screen that survives it. Notice which answers the whole room argues about, because those are the cases a static mockup was hiding.

That’s the workshop now, and the door is open to anyone willing to write a few lines of sampling code.
